After one round of hardware sampling, followed by classical ranking and recovery of the cached counts with the molecular Hamiltonian and no further QPU calls, 27 of 28 runs at 46-70 qubits are within 15 mHa of the density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) reference (median 4.5 mHa), and in all eight runs with an untrained control the trained policy is more accurate. At 56-70 qubits the selected circuits use 34-72 times fewer two-qubit gates than the local unitary cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) circuit transpiled for the same device. These results demonstrate that circuit generators can be trained with quantum hardware at 70 qubits.

title: Omni-JEV: Text and Dual-Stream Speech Decisions
authors: Shengzhou Kong
abstract: A user utterance does not uniquely determine the next action in full-duplex dialogue: its consequences depend on the assistant's response state and interaction history. Speech activity, utterance completion, and interruption intent provide related evidence, whose implications for a response require an explicit action policy. We formulate this task at collected-segment endpoints and introduce Omni-JEV, which maps text or role-indexed user and assistant-reference speech to probabilities over five interaction actions. An aligned speech-to-speech understanding backbone encodes the acoustic roles separately and shares its candidate readout with text inputs. Bilingual weak supervision supports cross-entropy fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning for probability-sensitive decisions (RLCD). We compare Gaussian-logit and categorical Choice RLCD from the same supervised initialization under matched training exposure, observing different trade-offs between classification and probability quality. Gaussian Omni-JEV achieves test accuracies of 84.08% for audio and 96.55% for text. This common action interface supports decisions about when a full-duplex voice assistant should respond, preserve ongoing speech, interrupt, or resume an interrupted response.

title: LLM Validation Makes Minimal-Pair Benchmarks Easier for Language Models
authors: Guofang Tang, Zheng Qu
abstract: Minimal-pair benchmarks are only as good as their labels, and LLMs are an obvious substitute for costly human validation. We test it on BLiMP (English) and QFrBLiMP (Quebec French), the two public minimal-pair datasets releasing every forced-choice human judgment. Three LLMs validate by forced choice, by rating, and as a panel, scored against human panels of one, three and five judges in two pre-registered phases. On BLiMP, forced-choice validators agree with held-out human majorities more often than five-judge panels, yet catch far fewer pairs whose label humans reject than one judge does. By point estimate, no validator is worth more than one judge. The errors are not random. On both datasets, across 10 open LMs, human-supported pairs that the pre-registered LLM filter flags are 18.9 points harder than those it accepts, in all 70 LM-validator combinations, and harder than pairs a single human judge flags. Filtering thus removes items on which LMs fail but humans do not, raising accuracy more than random removal. A protocol frozen before any output replicates the gap and the lift on Dutch BLiMP-NL. LLM validation makes minimal-pair benchmarks easier for the models they are meant to test; we release code, validator outputs and item-level scores.

title: Are Causal Neuron Circuits Unique and Transferable?
authors: \"Omer Tekin Yavuz (\.Ileti\c{s}im Yaz{\i}l{\i}m)
abstract: Interpretability demonstrations often show that intervening on a group of neurons changes a model's answer. A recent example removes an 18-neuron group in Qwen3-32B and the model answers "Simba" instead of "Scar" to a two-hop Lion King riddle. Such a demonstration establishes that the group matters, but not how much of it is necessary, whether other groups could do the same, or whether the effect carries over to other inputs. We ask: when intervening on a group of neurons changes a model's answer, how much of that group is actually necessary? For every selected group we measure all 4,096 subsets of 12 MLP neurons. On a two-alternative capital task (Qwen3-0.6B), zero-ablating 12 selected neurons lowers the answer margin by 27% while random neurons barely change it, yet replacing the same neurons with their values from other questions also barely changes it: their activations are nearly constant across questions, and we find no evidence that they carry question-specific content. On two-hop relation chains, patching 12 neurons with activations from the first-hop question shifts the answer to the bridge entity (from Scar to Simba): the greedy answer starts with the bridge in 9/11 chains for Qwen3-1.7B, 9/11 for Llama-3.2-1B and 8/10 for Gemma-3-1B; random neurons never do. The full group is rarely necessary: a few neurons often suffice, and in many chains disjoint subsets each flip the answer on their own, in an exploratory analysis most often when the model is less confident. Group effects transfer to rephrasings of the same chain but are much weaker on other tested chains. We study neuron-level causal interventions and alternative subsets; we do not recover the full connectivity of circuits.

title: Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II: Unlocking the Memory Potential of Pre-trained File Operations for Long-Horizon Tasks via On-Policy Distillation
authors: Lirui Luo, Kelong Mao, Xinwei Yang, Rongqing Li, Luyu Chen, Kieran Wong, Yudong Guo, Xinrui Wang, Jiayin Zhu, Pu Yao, Gu Simiu, Sulong Xu, Cong Fang
abstract: Language-model agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks whose interaction histories exceed the model's active context. They must therefore decide what to write down and what to read back, and when to do either. Recent work has begun to use on-policy distillation (OPD) to make memory control part of the policy, relying on memory tools and compaction protocols that lie outside either model's pre-training. However, this weakens the distillation on both sides: the teacher cannot give useful guidance on an interface it has never used, and the student samples too few meaningful memory actions for that guidance to take effect. To study this problem, we introduce Coding Agent Memory Gym II (CAMG-II), a suite of long-horizon agentic-RL environments spanning Shop, Coding, AutoResearch, General, and Visual. Alongside each environment's native task interface, CAMG-II provides ordinary Bash access and an episode-persistent workspace, enabling the policy to create, revise, search, and reuse files as memory across context replacements. We also introduce Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II (CAMP-II), which trains a single policy jointly across all five environments with fully asynchronous OPD to learn this file-based memory behavior directly from a frozen teacher with a prior for file operations. On CAMG-II, CAMP-II obtains 2.97 times the gain of the strongest OPD baseline. The memory behavior CAMP-II learns generalizes to two external benchmarks, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, with improved success rates.

title: Program-Aided Patchable Skill Evolution
authors: Jiahao Wang, Yuqi Xiong, Qing Yang, Zhipeng Xu, Zhenghao Liu, Zulong Chen, Yubin Bao
abstract: Agent skills have emerged as an effective means of enabling LLM agents to solve complex, interactive tasks by encoding reusable knowledge without modifying model parameters. Recent approaches further improve skill adaptation by distilling reusable experience from agent execution trajectories and evolving skills based on downstream task feedback. However, existing methods primarily represent skills as natural language documents, intertwining procedural logic with descriptive knowledge and making skills difficult to maintain and evolve. To address this limitation, we propose PASE (Program-Aided Patchable Skill Evolution), a program-aided framework that iteratively evolves skills by associating them with executable programs. Unlike prior approaches that encode trajectory-derived experience primarily in natural language, PASE separates reusable procedural logic into editable programs, enabling targeted updates to executable components while reducing the need to repeatedly revise natural language skills. Extensive experiments across diverse models and benchmarks demonstrate that PASE consistently outperforms all baselines, by achieving over 2.8% improvements. Further analyses show that PASE exhibits greater evolutionary stability and generalisation capability, highlighting the critical role of programmatic knowledge in skill evolution. We will release all data and code via GitHub.

title: An AI Assistant for Automating Anti-Corruption Expertise of Draft Legislation Based on the TRACE Framework
authors: Serhii Zabolotnii (Cherkasy State Business College, State Scientific Research Institute of Armament,Military Equipment Testing,Certification, Uzhhorod University), Alina Tarasova (Finport Technologies Inc. JSC")
abstract: We present an AI assistant for automating anti-corruption expertise of draft legislation based on the TRACE architecture, designed to screen bills for corruption risks: pinpoint provisions an expert would criticise and name the regulatory defect in each. The pipeline combines a deterministic parsing core, model-guided single-provision qualification, rule-based factor assignment, and external human oversight. To evaluate the assistant, we constructed an open benchmark from the published conclusions of Ukraine's National Agency on Corruption Prevention (NAZK), comprising 132 draft laws with 474 model-extracted findings. A system flag agrees with a finding when it targets a compatible provision and an LLM judge rates the risk as the same (strict) or partly the same (lenient). On 100 draft laws, the pipeline matches 0.28 of the findings within its top ten flags using the local Gemma 4 31B model, 0.30 with Sonnet 5.5, and 0.43-0.46 across all flags (non-blind; the frozen blind baseline achieves 0.21, 95% CI 0.16-0.26). Across all runs, most misses occur on provisions that the system located but qualified as a different risk, and none of the 32 legal-collision findings was matched. On 21 acts held out from tuning, the pipeline outperforms a monolithic prompt containing the full methodology under the strict measure, though not under the lenient one, and Opus 5.5 adds nothing over Sonnet. The reported scores reflect agreement with model-extracted findings rated by an LLM judge whose two access routes agree on 73 of 74 labels, without human expert validation.

title: Ninety-Six Ways to Measure a Scribe: Fragmented Evaluation of Ambient Scribes in Healthcare
authors: Amama Mahmood, Shiye Cao, Laura Fleig, Junan Jiang, Theodore Jensen, Yee-Yin Choong, Kristen Greene, Chien-Ming Huang
abstract: Ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribes have moved rapidly from experimental pilots to enterprise-wide deployment across health systems, promising reduced documentation burden and improved clinician experience. While research evaluating these tools has expanded quickly, there are no agreed-upon protocols or standardized metrics for assessing their performance, making it difficult to compare findings or cumulatively synthesize evidence across studies. Across 54 recent evaluation studies, we identify ten evaluation dimensions and 40 distinct metrics, operationalized in 96 different ways-35 of them (36%) used by only a single study. Assessment is dominated by documentation efficiency and time, measured in 44 of 54 studies. The other dimensions appear at broadly similar rates (16-24 studies each), and safety and clinical outcome least consistently of all. Ripple effects on the broader care system, such as impact on patients' care outcomes, redistribution of work, changes in billing and coding intensity, and downstream use of notes by other clinicians are rarely assessed. Moreover, the metrics used rely heavily on self-report and are fragmented and inconsistently operationalized, which limits comparability and hinders synthesis across studies. As an effort to support more rigorous and cumulative evaluation, in this paper we review the study designs, data sources, and metrics commonly used to evaluate ambient AI scribes in healthcare settings, discuss the limitations of current evaluation practice, and argue for a more holistic approach grounded in a standardized, multi-dimensional set of metrics.

title: Accurate predictions of properties of energetic materials with tabular foundation models
authors: Vagn Krister Nes Glomsrud, Mathias Bynke, Lars Henry Berge Olsen, Dennis Christensen
abstract: We use TabPFN, a recently developed tabular foundation model, to predict three properties of energetic materials: impact sensitivity, decomposition temperature and crystal density. Without any hyperparameter tuning, TabPFN outperforms the best published models for all three properties. It also substantially outperforms a wide range of established machine-learning models, including tuned gradient boosting (XGBoost), random forests and Gaussian processes. This holds both when the models are given hand-crafted molecular descriptors and when they are given learned representations from Chemprop's message-passing neural network. In particular, for all three properties, TabPFN applied to Chemprop's own embedding is more accurate than Chemprop's predictions. TabPFN is also among the fastest models we consider, more than an order of magnitude faster than XGBoost. As TabPFN predicts the entire distribution of the target rather than just a single value, it offers built-in uncertainty quantification, which we compare with the empirical distributions of compounds with repeated measurements. Finally, we interpret the predictions using Shapley values, which rank the features by their importance.

title: Continual-ARC: Measuring Skill Acquisition over a Working Lifetime
authors: Daniel Lenton, Yusha Arif, Haris Mahmood
abstract: Agent harnesses have emerged as a promising mechanism for continual learning, alongside test-time parametric learning. However, the current benchmarks have several limitations: they generally focus on a single applied domain, serve each instance only once, and assume a single family of learner, so memory-based and weight-based systems are rarely compared on the same scale. We propose Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream built from the three ARC-AGI editions, whose tasks need no domain knowledge. The same tasks return after dormant gaps with fresh instances, while new tasks keep arriving. On each instance, the learner may pay for demonstrations, submit answers, or act inside the harness, with retries permitted on incorrect submissions, which are paid for. Each instance is scored based on the share of this feedback budget consumed. Since a learner may keep anything between instances, memory-based and weight-based systems are scored on the same scale. After the stream, the learner is frozen and tested on fresh instances of the tasks it met, which measures memorization, and on unseen tasks, which measures generalization. We run an agent harness with frozen weights, with and without persistence, on Qwen3.5-9B and GLM-5.3 Flash, comparing them with two prompting floors, a program-induction method and Qwen3.5-9B's weights trained to imitate GLM-5.3 Flash. Persistence in the harness generally does not improve memorization unless provided with explicit expert guidance. Most harness-based methods still learn less than a floor that simply caches each task's demonstrations, across all models we tested. No harness-based method gains on unseen tasks, whereas weight-based learning shows substantial gains. This opens the door to future weight-based continual learning that could teach models to drive harnesses in new domains.

title: Care, Human Enfeeblement, and the Existential Implications of AGI
authors: B. Scot Rousse
abstract: Stuart Russell has named "human enfeeblement" as a long-term societal risk of advanced AI. This paper gives a new interpretation of the enfeeblement danger by interpreting it in light of recent work by Brian Christian, Alison Gopnik, and David Spivak on care and caregiving, and connecting it with the ontological design tradition of Terry Winograd and Fernando Flores. The enfeeblement that threatens is not merely a matter of cognitive off-loading and loss of knowledge, but a form of disengagement with the world which I explain in terms of an erosion of our capacities to care. This paper articulates a conception of care as a constellation of cultivable skills that involve us in the world and with each other, while making life worth living. Designing AI to support our capacities to care addresses the worry recently raised by Demis Hassabis and others regarding the questions of "meaning and purpose" that are looming in a post-AGI world.

title: Null-Corrected Conditional Coverage in Materials Property Prediction: A Five-Dataset Replication
authors: Irene Boruah
abstract: Uncertainty quantification for materials property prediction increasingly reports conditional coverage, coverage within strata of the predicted value, alongside marginal coverage. The worst-bin statistics used for this are downward-biased in finite samples, a known defect that applied materials work does not generally correct for. We replicate a single-dataset conditional coverage study across five regression datasets (n = 437 to 21,263), seven interval methods and 50 random splits each, correcting the worst-bin statistic against its expected value under exact conditional validity. The null is simulated from realized per-bin test counts and referenced to each method's own marginal coverage, separating marginal miscalibration from uneven coverage. On the smallest dataset the correction runs from 0.061 to 0.096, between a third and two thirds of the shortfalls actually reported, against 0.009 to 0.011 on the two largest. Split conformal prediction's failure survives the correction on four of five datasets; two conclusions of the antecedent study do not. Conformalized quantile regression, characterized there as a negative case, fails on one dataset only. Cross-fitted normalized conformal prediction, grouped there with the successful methods, fails on three of five. Group-conditional (Mondrian) conformal prediction stays below our significance criterion on every dataset, yet exceeds the null on three of five under an octile refinement of the variable it calibrates on. A level-matched ablation locates that uniformity in group-conditional calibration rather than in the elevated quantile level, and removes Mondrian's apparent width cost entirely. Conditional coverage evaluations should report the null distribution of the worst-bin statistic used, the method's realized marginal coverage, and the resolution of the evaluation partition relative to any partition the method calibrates on.

title: EasyFoam: Skill-Oriented OpenFOAM Agents with Evidence-Driven Evolution
authors: Peng Yin, Zhiwei Chen, Tianyi Liu, Chen Li, Kai Li, Jian Cheng
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly capable of automating end-to-end OpenFOAM workflows for computational fluid dynamics (CFD). However, current progress is bottlenecked by two critical limitations. First, existing evaluations are dominated by tutorial-level cases and execution-oriented metrics, masking a substantial executability--acceptability gap: successfully executed simulations often fail to satisfy prescribed numerical or quantity-of-interest (QoI) criteria. Second, domain expertise in existing systems is tightly coupled with bespoke agent architectures, limiting its reuse and continual refinement across agent implementations. To address these challenges, we introduce ExtFoamBench, a challenging benchmark for OpenFOAM agents that spans five axes of workflow variation, and separately assesses execution completion, numerical soundness, and QoI satisfaction. Complementing this, we propose EasyFoam, an agent framework that decouples CFD expertise into modular, externalized skills driven by a dual-loop mechanism. An execution loop constructs workflows from explicit task requirements and uses structured simulation evidence to diagnose failures and guide targeted repairs. Meanwhile, an evolution loop distills task experience into reusable skill updates selected through paired evaluation. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that EasyFoam achieves substantially higher task acceptance rates than baseline agents, establishing this work as a starting point for future research toward self-improving CFD agents.

title: Partial pooling beats synthetic respondents as estimators, not as covariates: a preregistered small-sample tournament
authors: Howard Kim
abstract: Survey estimates for population segments, such as media use by sex and age, rest on few respondents per cell, and a growing literature offers synthetic respondents generated by large language models to fill the gap. That literature has not tested them against the small-area estimators a methodologist would otherwise use. We ran ten estimators, preregistered, on identical household-clustered splits of a Korean media panel across five calibration budgets and three holdout regimes. A multilevel partial-pooling model of the MRP family led every calibration-only estimator at every budget, matching at one hundred respondents what direct estimation reaches with roughly four times as many. On unobserved segments, information fixed as a per-segment prior was inert for synthetic panel and previous wave alike; attached as a bias correction it transferred, at the price of estimation noise. No registered synthetic advantage over MRP survived the paired decision rule. Entered instead as a covariate inside the multilevel model, an exploratory hybrid, the same panel improved on MRP on unobserved segments: the information survives where the registered constructions did not. Interval coverage stayed below nominal throughout and worsened with budget for partial pooling, contrary to prediction.

title: Credal Wrapper for Uncertainty Modelling in Sparse Geological Data
authors: David Jeevankumar, Maryam Sultana, Alexander D. Rast, Fabio Cuzzolin
abstract: Machine learning models for mineral exploration are trained on a few hundred sparse, expensive samples and used to decide where to drill next, so their epistemic uncertainty (EU), the part that more data could remove, matters as much as their predictions. Yet EU cannot be measured on real data, because the counterfactual that defines it is never observed, so estimators are graded by proxies such as out-of-distribution detection and calibration. We contribute a general simulation protocol that makes EU directly computable for a given model and can grade any EU estimator. It separates two estimands the literature conflates, reducible error and estimator spread, builds an oracle reference for each in a synthetic prospectivity field sampled by clustered drilling surveys, and compares uncertainty measures of an identical ensemble within each simulated world. We use it to ask when credal (imprecise-probability) measures are more faithful than Bayesian model averaging (BMA) in the sparse, low-class regime of geological classification. The credal interval width recovers the epistemic ordering better than BMA when members are few, confirming the small-ensemble advantage reported for credal wrappers; the advantage vanishes by M = 10 and reverses at M = 40. Secondly, the choice of credal functional matters more than the choice between credal and BMA. Lastly, the credal advantage does not widen as training data are thinned, so it compensates for few posterior samples rather than few data. On real drill-hole geochemistry from South Australia, a resampling oracle reproduces the first finding. The protocol applies to any EU estimator whose data-generating process can be simulated.

title: Clustering trajectories of modelled estimates: an uncertainty-aware framework, with an application to global cardiovascular disease burden, 1990 to 2023
authors: Eben Afrifa-Yamoah
abstract: Modelled health estimates such as those of the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study are increasingly used in secondary analyses designed for observed data. However, trajectory clustering typically ignores published uncertainty, selects the number of clusters using criteria blind to it, and assigns countries to groups with unwarranted certainty. We propose an uncertainty-aware framework that separates trajectory level from shape, quantifies membership probabilities by perturbing estimates within their uncertainty intervals, selects clusters based on stability under uncertainty, and examines the roles of development, region, and measurement quality. Applied to age-standardised cardiovascular disease DALY rates for 201 countries from 1990-2023 (GBD 2023), the framework identified two stable trajectory types, whereas the gap statistic selected three. The additional cluster was poorly supported (median membership probability 0.70) and disappeared once uncertainty was considered. The retained clusters had similar burdens in 1990 but diverged markedly over time: a stalled-improvement group of 78 countries (median change $-8\%$, 40 of them in sub-Saharan Africa) and a sustained-decline group of 92 countries ($-52\%$). Thirty-one countries remained unclassified because their memberships were uncertain. Results were reproduced using mortality rates, a 2000-2023 analysis window, and bootstrap resampling. Among countries with the narrowest uncertainty intervals, a third well-supported trajectory emerged in former Soviet and Eastern European countries. These findings show that uncertainty affects both the number and composition of trajectory clusters. Ignoring it risks over-interpreting unstable groups and overstating confidence in country classifications. Incorporating published uncertainty and measurement quality should become standard practice when clustering modelled health estimates.

title: Enhancing Resolution and Reliability with Attention Mechanisms in Nuclear Accident Surrogate Modeling
authors: Wonung Jeong, Sangam Khanal, Jeongik Lee, Sangseung Lee, Joongoo Jeon
abstract: Severe accident (SA) analysis of nuclear power plants relies on system codes such as MAAP, whose computational cost limits large-scale applications including dynamic probabilistic safety assessment and reinforcement learning. This study proposes the Accident Binary-Continuous Transformer (ABC-Transformer), a decoder-only surrogate combining causal self-attention with temporal attention pooling. It jointly embeds continuous thermal-hydraulic variables with binary safety-system and severe accident management guideline (SAMG) states, enabling 5-minute-resolution forecasting over 72-hour transients. Trained on 11,000 MAAP simulations of a total loss of component cooling water scenario for the OPR1000, it achieved lower one-step teacher-forcing error than CNN and recurrent baselines at fine resolutions. Autoregressive reliability was characterized as a full per-scenario distribution over 1100 held-out scenarios. For scheduled-sampling (SS) training, the median $R^2$ is $0.947 \pm 0.006$ and $3.8 \pm 1.0$% of scenarios fail ($R^2<0$; mean $\pm$ SD over four training seeds), while errors accumulate with rollout length. A Mahalanobis self-distance computed from each surrogate rollout, before comparison with the MAAP reference, ranks these failures (ROC-AUC 0.895, reference seed). A threshold at the 40th percentile of calibration scores accepts $36.8 \pm 0.5$% of 550 evaluation scenarios, with no accepted rollout below $R^2 = 0$ for any seed, and routes the rest to MAAP.

title: Quantifying Methodological Inflation in Clinical Machine Learning: A Cross-Modality Audit of Subject-Level Leakage and Nested Feature Selection for Parkinson's Disease
authors: Namrata Datta, Victor Miranda Soberanis
abstract: Reported accuracy in Parkinson's disease (PD) machine learning can reflect the evaluation protocol rather than real signal. We ask how much evaluation choices inflate performance by comparing naive and rigorous protocols on voice, telemonitoring and blood-transcriptomic datasets. Subject-aware splitting reduced voice AUROC from 0.892 to 0.780 and telemonitoring R^2 from 0.105 to -0.037; Random Forest recovered neither gap. Supervised probe selection before splitting inflated transcriptomic AUROC from 0.711 to 0.998. A nested 50-probe panel matched a 1,000-probe panel (0.811 versus 0.844), and recruitment-wave batch structure was detected. Future work should validate a stable panel on an independent cohort.

title: Learning Nonlinear Transient Dynamics in Fluid Flow Networks with the Neural Basis Method
authors: Aijaz Nazir, Yuhe Wang, S. K. Rasel, Min Wang
abstract: Fluid flow networks, from pipeline infrastructure to biological vasculature, are governed by nonlinear edgewise hyperbolic laws coupled through continuity and conservation at junctions. Many-query tasks require rapid evaluation across unseen parametric settings, but conventional methods re-solve the system for each query at prohibitive cost. Existing physics-informed neural approaches impose the governing equations through penalty losses over generic neural approximators; these losses act only as optimization surrogates, with no guarantee that their reduction reduces solution error, and the resulting optimization is prone to ill-conditioning, particularly for hyperbolic systems. Building on the "representation-then-projection" principle of the neural basis method, we introduce a new approach for modeling fluid flow networks. Fixed neural bases define the representation space on each edge, while projection of the discretized equations determines the expansion coefficients, embedding edgewise laws into a conservative formulation. Edge subdomains are coupled through non-overlapping domain decomposition, and a neural operator learns, directly in this reduced space, the parametric map to the expansion coefficients. On looped and branching network topologies, we reproduce references with relative $L^2$ errors below 0.02%, whereas the physics-informed neural network baseline fails. Across unseen boundary conditions in both interpolation and extrapolation, we maintain mean pressure errors below 1% and mean flux errors below 3.3%, while the physics-informed DeepONet baseline reaches 8-18% pressure errors and 85-95% flux errors. These results highlight the framework's potential for real-time monitoring, design exploration, and uncertainty quantification of fluid flow networks.

title: Gaussian processes for real-time urban traffic estimation using a fleet of drones
authors: Batuhan Avci, Marko Susnjar, Marko Maljkovic, Nikolas Geroliminis
abstract: Real-time urban traffic monitoring is essential for modern city management, yet conventional static sensors provide only limited spatial coverage. Autonomous drone fleets can complement this infrastructure by offering flexible, high-resolution mobile sensing across different parts of the network. This paper introduces a spatio-temporal Gaussian process (GP) framework for reconstructing network-wide traffic states from partial aerial observations. The model accounts for the physical structure of the road network through a graph Mat\'ern kernel, which embeds network topology into the spatial covariance structure, and captures temporal dependencies through an exponential temporal kernel. Within this framework, historical loop detector data provide an informative prior mean that is updated in real time using incoming drone observations, yielding network-wide point estimates together with predictive uncertainty. We validate our framework in two distinct case studies: a microscopic simulation of Barcelona and real-world drone data from Athens. The results demonstrate that our approach outperforms historical baselines in estimating and predicting Vehicle Hours Traveled (VHT), notably reducing the required fleet size. Furthermore, leveraging the model's predictive uncertainty to guide drone movements yields additional performance gains, highlighting the potential for future uncertainty-aware fleet routing algorithms.

title: Modeling Drug Overdose Mortality Levels Using Social Vulnerability Indicators in U.S. Counties: A Double Machine Learning Approach for Causal Analysis
authors: Qunhui Guo, Jiongbai Liu, Md Noor E Alam
abstract: Drug poisoning mortality (DPM) remains a leading cause of death among working-age Americans, and its burden falls unevenly across communities. Existing county-level studies of social vulnerability and overdose have largely reported predictive or associational relationships, while the shape of the adjusted exposure-response relationship between overall social vulnerability and mortality remains unclear. We examined the CDC/ATSDR Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) and county drug poisoning mortality across three two-year windows spanning 2016-2021. The associational analysis compared linear regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost models of log mortality using period-specific SVI subfeatures and county covariates. The selected XGBoost models were interpreted with SHAP values. The double machine learning (DML) analysis estimated the exposure-response relationship between SVI and DPM and tested the linearity restriction. Socioeconomic vulnerability contributed positively to predicted mortality, with disability and unemployment among the strongest subfeatures, while racial and ethnic minority composition contributed negatively in all three periods. Summing the four theme contributions reduced the overall-index attribution by 34% to 36%, indicating substantial offsetting. Linearity was rejected in every window ($p < 10^{-26}$). The adjusted relationship increased through the middle of the SVI distribution and declined in the upper tail. This pattern remained stable both before and after the outbreak of the epidemic. Overall SVI therefore captured meaningful variation in overdose mortality but did not function as a uniformly increasing risk scale across its full range. Component-level interpretation and current overdose surveillance provide important context for interpreting the composite index.

title: Can a search hold its own bar? In-loop deflation and its exploits in autonomous strategy discovery
authors: Eray Gen\c{c}ay
abstract: Corrections for backtest overfitting such as the deflated Sharpe ratio are applied after a search ends: the searcher maximises raw performance and a separate procedure deflates the reported winner. Autonomous searches driven by large language models perform many implicit backtests before reporting, so this paper asks what changes when the correction moves inside the loop and the acceptance threshold is indexed to the running count and dispersion of the search's own trials. The threshold then becomes an object the search can optimise against: we show analytically that a naive in-loop bar admits a variance-dilution effect, in which mediocre near-duplicate candidates lower the bar because the ledger's dispersion falls faster than its trial-count factor grows. We propose two defences, a pre-registered variance floor and a monotone high-water-mark bar, and evaluate the construction under a protocol frozen before any run, with every in-loop decision replaying exactly from its recorded trace. Across 53 audited hundred-candidate searches over two frontier models, two universes, and two feature spaces, the gated search reports "no certifiable discovery" on 36 of 37 runs, un-gated controls report a strategy on all 16, and every arm's out-of-sample confidence interval includes zero. Supporting studies find that state-based stopping reaches the same outcome after 8 to 9 trials at about a twelfth of the trial budget while an adaptive budget adds nothing, that a controlled stress test reproduces the dilution effect and both defences, and that a hundred nominal trials collapse to 6 to 8 effectively independent return streams. We scope these results to the analysed system.

title: Katz Kernel Based Stratification of Breast Cancer Patients
authors: Francesco Cellitti, Lorenzo Di Rocco, Livia Perfetto, Veronica Lombardo, Umberto Ferraro Petrillo
abstract: The integration of mechanistic signaling networks into clinical research has become a cornerstone of precision oncology. By capturing the complex biochemical interactions within a cell, these networks provide a functional map of disease progression that goes beyond simple genomic mutations. Consequently, the development of specific signaling models of patients has significant relevance, allowing for a more granular representation of individual disease profiles. In this setting, there is a growing need for robust methodologies capable of comparing graph based pathway structures to identify similarities and differences across patient cohorts. Such comparisons are essential for the identification of clinically meaningful subgroups, and the discovery of novel biomarkers. Standard graph kernels, while mathematically rigorous, often remain too generic for this purpose. They frequently fail to capture features specific to gene signaling networks, resulting in suboptimal clustering performance. In this paper, we present a domain specific graph kernel designed for mechanistic signaling networks. Unlike generic approaches, our method explicitly incorporates biological constraints and gene interaction patterns into the kernel formulation, enabling a more accurate characterization of both topological structure and functional behavior. We assess its performance on breast cancer datasets, focusing on its ability to support disease subtyping. Our results suggest that our approach can effectively contribute to patient stratification.

title: Modelling the occurrence and reporting dynamics of weather-related home insurance claims
authors: Paul Wilsens, Katrien Antonio, Gerda Claeskens, Koos Gubbels
abstract: We study the occurrence and reporting dynamics of weather-related claims in private home insurance, combining detailed portfolio and claim information with publicly available high-resolution weather data. Existing approaches typically start from an identified severe weather event, such as a hailstorm, and model the dynamics of the claims caused by that event. In practice, however, claims arise under moderate as well as severe conditions, and the claims handling process runs continuously. An insurer therefore requires insight into the occurrence and reporting of claims on every calendar day. Modelling all calendar days jointly poses two challenges: recently occurred claims are only partially reported, and days with severe weather are rare while accounting for a large share of the claims. We propose a multi-regime EM-XGBoost framework that addresses both: an expectation-maximisation setup accounts for the incurred-but-not-reported (IBNR) claims, while a data-driven regime structure lets the occurrence and reporting dynamics differ across weather conditions. In a case study on a Dutch home insurance portfolio, we compare single- and two-regime specifications for two spatial resolutions: the country as a whole, and its individual regions. We find that the regional two-regime model outperforms the regional single-regime model as well as both national models, indicating that the benefit of a multi-regime setting depends on a sufficiently granular spatial resolution. We also show that daily covariates constructed from hourly weather observations, capturing the duration and the intra-day timing of severe weather, improve both the occurrence and the reporting model.

title: Zugwise: Domain-Aware Game Reconstruction for Digitizing Handwritten Chess Scoresheets
authors: Gerhard Trippen (University of Toronto)
abstract: Digitizing handwritten chess scoresheets has been studied as a handwriting-recognition problem: read the move in each box and check that it is legal. This framing misses the errors that matter most. A misread that yields an illegal move is loud. One that yields a legal-but-wrong move is silent, because a legality-only pipeline accepts it and reads every later move against a wrong position. We therefore treat the task as game reconstruction and present Zugwise, which repurposes computer-chess machinery (quiescence search, static exchange evaluation, pin detection) to ask not "what should be played?" but "could a human plausibly have written this?" An absurdity detector makes silent errors loud at or near where they occur, and a backward search traces late symptoms to their cause. Candidate ranking excludes chess-quality signals. A Needleman-Wunsch merge adds the second player's sheet as evidence, and review stops send every disagreement between the sheets' legal readings to a human. In oracle replay of two tournament sections, a release adding them cuts silent errors from 16 to 1 and from 50 to 13. Two learned signals, CTC re-scoring against the recognizer's raw output and a Maia-style human-move prior, raise the correct fix's top-rank rate from 58.8% to 78.0% of the replacement decisions where it is a candidate, and hold without refitting on a later section. On the first section, the human-verified output matches an independent expert transcription move for move on 34 of 45 games, and adjudication against the sheets found errors in both records, on different plies. We do not establish that either workflow is faster or more accurate. The system runs entirely in the browser and is free, private, and offline-capable; alongside it we offer a three-way adjudication protocol for a domain where no single record is ground truth.

title: metalSPARSE: A 2:4 Semi-Structured Sparse GEMV Kernel for Apple Silicon GPUs
authors: Tek Raj Awasthi (Friedrich-Alexander-Universit\"at Erlangen-N\"urnberg), Babita Awasthi
abstract: Autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs) generate text one token at a time, and each token reads every weight from memory, so on edge devices, decoding is limited by memory bandwidth. 2:4 semi-structured sparsity keeps two of every four weights, but Apple-silicon GPUs have no sparse matrix hardware, so pruning helps only if a kernel actually reads fewer bytes. We present metalSPARSE, to our knowledge the first 2:4 sparse kernels for Apple GPUs, together with a fused decoder written in Metal. The kernels stream weights in compressed form and expand them in registers. On Qwen2.5-1.5B with 2:4 sparsity on every decoder linear layer, decoding runs 3.6x faster than HuggingFace Transformers on PyTorch-MPS on an 8 GB M2 MacBook Air and 1.52x faster than MLX on a 16 GB M4. The same engine on dense weights matches MLX, so the gain comes from the compressed weights, and sparsity delivers 97% of the speedup its byte reduction allows. Prompt processing, which is compute-bound, does not speed up. To preserve quality, we combine a Wanda mask with block-wise reconstruction and low-rank adapters trained jointly with the surviving weights and quantized to 4 bits. On WikiText-2 this brings perplexity from 3.01x dense after one-shot pruning (Wanda with a closed-form refit) to 1.34x, and the whole pipeline runs on the same laptop/hardware.

title: SideTaskBench: Measuring Unauthorized Side-Task Delivery in Coding Agents
authors: Xiangyu Wen, Qiang Xu
abstract: Can a coding agent fix a user's repository while also completing and delivering work the user never requested? In this paper, we introduce SideTaskBench to measure this failure where third-party technical references induce agents to produce independent side-task artifacts during an authorized repair. Repair success alone misses this behavior. Our key measurement contribution is to pair each repair with a self-contained side task and verify side tasks' delivery success rate along with the repair success rate. The benchmark contains 25 Python repairs and 190 side-task units. Its four-level similarity index defines 300 executable repair--side-task pairs. The experiments show roughly 40% valid delivery under wrapped requests for two models, alongside repair success close to their clean baselines. The completed v10 similarity run uses DeepSeek-V4-Flash on all 300 pairs, with eight repetitions per pair (2,400 runs). Conditional delivery ranges from 20.48% for L0 unrelated tasks to 57.44% for L3 mechanism-overlapping tasks, while the L1-L0 difference is 5.37 percentage points and remains sensitive to task composition. The central insight is that technical relevance may blur the authorization boundary for an agent, such that an agent can solve the requested problem and still deliver unauthorized work. SideTaskBench emphasizes this potential weakness of existing agents and provides a testbed for defenses that preserve repair capability while preventing unauthorized delivery. The code is available at: https://github.com/xywen97/SideTaskBench.

title: Probe Before You Preach: Conformal Ambiguity Sets and Neuro-Symbolic Counterfactual Probing for Diagnosing Algebraic Misconceptions in Middle School Mathematics
authors: Caihong Xu, Xiangyu Yu
abstract: Distinct mathematical misconception rules can produce the same incorrect answer, making diagnosis from a single response ambiguous. We formalize this algebraic collision and derive a conditional Bayes error bound; internally generated reasoning does not add student-specific information beyond its inputs under an explicit conditional-independence assumption. We propose Mondrian Adaptive Conformal Misconception Sets (MACMS) and Symbolic-Verified Counterfactual Micro-Probing (Sym-EIG). MACMS has curriculum-group marginal coverage under exchangeability, not a per-student correctness guarantee. Sym-EIG searches for probes whose outputs separate modeled candidate rules; identification additionally depends on the candidate set and response model. An audit of a local public Eedi graph finds 2,118 of 2,258 linked constructs associated with at least two misconception IDs; construct-level associations alone do not establish same-answer collisions. Other project performance tables require recomputation because their script assigns numerical results directly. No diagnostic performance or classroom learning benefit is claimed here. A classroom study is proposed for future validation.

title: AVA: Agentic Variant Adjudication for Automated, Auditable Read-Level Review in Cancer Diagnostic Sequencing
authors: Caleb Chin, Sidharth Gupta, Arun K Anguraj Vadivel, Robert Siddaway, Siddharth Arya, Arianna He, Peter Zhukovsky, Cynthia Hawkins
abstract: Identifying a tumor's DNA mutations is central to cancer diagnosis and treatment, but distinguishing genuine mutations from sequencing artifacts is error-prone. In practice, genuine mutations are identified using fixed variant-allele-frequency (VAF) and depth thresholds which cannot separate artifacts from genuine mutations in the borderline low-VAF zone where they overlap. A laboratory specialist must manually inspect the read-level sequencing data, a slow step that has high inter-rater variability and causes diagnosis delays. We present AVA: Agentic Variant Adjudication; an agentic framework that automates this read-level inspection with subagents that reason over evidence, generate investigative code, and return a real-or-artifact adjudications with an auditable reasoning trace all without training on existing data. On both the SEQC2 DNA-seq benchmark and patient RNA-seq data, restricted to a subsample of borderline variants where thresholds fail, both closed-source (Claude Sonnet 5) and open-weight (GLM 5.3 Flash and Gemma 4 31b) agents outperform the best achievable VAF/depth thresholds. Ultimately, AVA is suited for privacy-constrained clinical deployment, since the framework can run on locally deployed open-weight models with descriptive reasoning traces to keep specialists in the loop.

title: Provenance-tracked, experimentally validated neural operator surrogates of three-dimensional laser melting with keyholes and free-form paths
authors: Alix Benoit (Light-Matter Dynamics Group, Laboratory for Multifunctional Materials,Interfaces, Empa), Elia Iseli (Light-Matter Dynamics Group, Laboratory for Multifunctional Materials,Interfaces, Empa)
abstract: A three-dimensional thermo-fluid-dynamic simulation of laser melting resolves the melt pool and vapor depression but costs from one to thousands of core-hours per track. We train FNO, RIGNO and GAOT neural operators that predict the temperature, melt-pool and free-surface fields. Our datasets comprise 3D temperature and melt geometry fields covering lack-of-fusion to keyhole conditions under varied laser power, scan speed, beam radius, beam shape and preheat, and include free-form scan paths with speed changes and up to four beams. We generate them with FLOW-3D WELD, using solver settings validated against published measurements for four materials. We implement an AiiDA framework to store the provenance of every simulation, model and evaluation, so each tabulated metric traces back to the solver and model inputs behind it. On held-out simulations, the best architecture scores below 2 % relative temperature error on quasi-steady straight tracks, below 4 % on single-beam free-form paths and about 5 % with two to four beams. Inference takes under a second per predicted arbitrary time step on our single-GPU setup. We extend a surrogate trained on Ti-6Al-4V to Inconel 718 by growing its training set autonomously, and the extended models reach a relative temperature error of about 3 % or less on both Inconel 718 and Ti-6Al-4V. At 20 Ti-6Al-4V and Inconel 718 conditions held out of training, the two-alloy RIGNO predicts melt-pool and vapor-depression depths within 30 % of published measurements, and its depths differ from FLOW-3D at the same conditions by 2 % on average. Furthermore, these results provide a scalable framework which can readily be applied to computationally intensive simulations in fields other than laser melting.

title: Deep learning-guided discovery reveals the diversity and mutational potential of environmental beta-lactamases
authors: Liangjun Ge, Qiandi Gao, Haiming Xu, Zhiwei Qin, Heqian Zhang
abstract: Beta-lactamases are a major mechanism of bacterial resistance to beta-lactam antibiotics; however, their functional diversity and mutational potential in environmental microbial communities remain partially understood. This study aimed to characterize environmental beta-lactamase diversity and investigate how sequence variation influences antibiotic resistance. By integrating protein language model (PLMs) with ensemble learning, we identified more than 46,000 putative beta-lactamases across all four Ambler classes from environmental metagenomes, widely distributed across diverse habitats, with distinct habitat-associated class compositions. The candidates sharing approximately 30% sequence identity with known beta-lactamases conferred resistance to multiple beta-lactam antibiotics when expressed in Escherichia coli. Combining inverse folding model with PLMs further identified mutations that altered resistance profiles, including substitutions that increased resistance to carbapenems. Predicted high-fitness sites exhibited greater natural sequence variability overall, with higher variability in wastewater-derived than ocean-derived enzymes. These findings reveal undercharacterized beta-lactamase diversity and substantial mutational flexibility in environmental microbiomes, providing a basis for investigating their potential contribution to the diversification of antibiotic resistance.

title: MechFoundry: An agentic loop that poses and performs engineering analyses and optimization of real-world objects
authors: Xue-Ling Luo, Marco Conte, Peter Yichen Chen, Nikolaos Bouklas
abstract: AI agents can automate software engineering because a compiler or a test suite checks that the code does what the user or the agent intended. In engineering analysis, however, the steps that precede the computation have few easily verifiable checks: modeling a design or an object, deciding how it is used, where supports and loads are applied, and what material each part is made of. A human expert therefore makes these decisions, carries out the steps, and judges the result, one object at a time. We present MechFoundry, an agentic loop coupled with bespoke software that automates structural analyses of real-world objects without a human in the loop. From an object's lexical description, it generates a shape, poses a loading case relevant to how the object is used, assigns a material to each part, solves the nonlinear structural response, and improves the design against the loads it carries. A differentiable GPU solver built on an adaptive octree that need not conform to the surface enables the transition from shape generation to simulation and optimization. Across 50 everyday and engineering objects, the agent posed and solved a loading case in 6.5 minutes and for US$1.3 per object on average. Without a test suite to check against, we had language-model reviewers grade each session, as a first indication of where the agent's engineering judgment holds and where it fails.

title: Beyond the First Hit: Towards Tight Guarantees for $k$-means++
authors: Aravind Reddy
abstract: Let $R_k$ be the worst-case ratio between the expected cost of the $k$ seeds chosen by $k$-means++ and the optimal $k$-means cost. In their seminal paper introducing $k$-means++, Arthur and Vassilvitskii (SODA 2007) showed that $2\ln k\le R_k\le8(\ln k+2)$, and Makarychev, Reddy and Shan (NeurIPS 2020) improved the upper bound to $5(\ln k+2)$. We prove $R_k\le\frac{1163}{233}+2.108\,H_{k-2}$ for every $k\ge3$ by a computer-assisted argument, and $R_k\le5+2.3139\,H_{k-2}$ for every $k\ge2$ by a short analytic argument; here $H_j$ is the $j$th harmonic number. Since $H_{k-2}\le1+\ln k$, this lowers the leading coefficient of $\ln k$ from $5$ to $2.108$. We also determine $R_2=5$ and $R_3=185/32$ exactly; both are suprema that are approached but not attained. On the lower side we prove $R_k\ge2(1+H_{k-1})$ for every $k$, and give a second family of lower bounds that is larger than this for $2\le k\le18$. Previous analyses bound the expected cost of a cluster just after it is first sampled by a constant times its optimal cost, and then charge that cost for the rest of the run. We instead track how a cluster's cost evolves after its first hit: a cluster left with a large residual cost is likely to be sampled again before it accumulates much of the logarithmic charge, and each repeat repairs it.

title: The norm, not the labels: training and evaluating finite-element surrogates for stress analysis in the energy norm
authors: Ruifeng Cao, Xidan Song
abstract: Finite-element surrogates predict the stresses of a new design in one evaluation, but are usually trained on solutions with a displacement loss and compared by it, although engineering decisions rest on stresses. Application in engineering: stress analysis of perforated plates and solids with cavities, parametric families in which holes concentrate stress. Contribution to artificial intelligence: training and evaluating such surrogates in the energy norm, with or without solutions, and screening their predictions without solutions. For linear elastostatics, minimising the assembled discrete potential energy is exactly supervised regression in this norm: the energy gap of a prediction is the strain energy of its stress error. A displacement loss under-weights the stiff modes that carry the strains. In pre-registered comparisons, changing only the norm of the supervised loss cut a three-dimensional transformer's median energy-norm error 7.5-fold and its median von Mises error 6.1-fold; in two dimensions it more than halved the von Mises error, also on held-out instances. In three dimensions, the transformer trained on the energy alone came within a factor of 1.3 of the energy-norm-supervised one in median energy-norm and von Mises error. It was more accurate than the displacement-supervised one on all five metrics in every seed. Given the stiffness matrix, a Ritz projection was more accurate than the label-free transformer, in the seed means, on every metric but peak stress. No network transferred to a substantially finer mesh. The energy ranks predictions of a load case, and its sign flags those worse than the zero field.

title: When Evaluators of AI Agents Disagree: An Empirical Study of Native Scoring, LLM Judges, and Commit-Boundary Checks on tau2-bench
authors: Sungbin Im
abstract: Agentic workflows, in which a large language model (LLM) calls tools to read and write data, are evaluated in two ways. Benchmarks compare the final state against a gold answer. Deployed services have none; an LLM judge reads the transcript and decides. Practice treats the two as interchangeable. This paper measures whether they are. We ran 2,160 episodes in tau2-bench's airline and retail domains and recorded every database write. We scored each episode four ways: native scoring against gold state, an LLM judge, that judge given the policy document, and the boundary evaluator, a minimal rule-based check of whether a write was expected against whether one occurred in the trace. Two annotators independently labeled 120 episodes for task correctness, policy compliance, and commitment correctness. The judge repeated its verdict 98.2% of the time but agreed with native scoring on 56.2%. In 11 episodes the agent executed a forbidden write. The judge passed 10 to 11, with or without the policy or transcript. A stronger judge still passed 6. The boundary evaluator, with no model call, caught all 11; no judge significantly exceeded it on human labels. Forbidden writes occurred in 11.1% of episodes without gates. Verification, correction, and safe-termination gates did not reduce them significantly. The traces show a candidate cause: the gates' evidence digest dropped the order status and customer authentication, so valid requests were rejected. The choice of evaluator decides the conclusion; the minimal check exposes failures the judges miss. Traces, code, prompts, and labels are released.

title: Finite-Cadence Refresh Equilibria for Streaming Prior-Anchored Ridge: A Closed-Form Forgetting Window and Spectral Correction
authors: Mrigank Shekhar Singh
abstract: Recursive estimators on drifting streams must forget stale data fast enough to track the target, yet slowly enough to average out noise. In prior-anchored ridge regression, this trade-off admits a closed-form spectral decomposition in which each eigen-direction interpolates between the data solution and the prior with pull weight $s_i = \rho / (\mu_i + \rho)$. When the anchor is refreshed every $k$ steps, we show that the moving-frame offset converges to a finite-cadence equilibrium that lags the pure-leaky path by an explicit $\Delta_k(s)$ while reducing estimation variance by a factor $\Psi(s, r_k)$. Minimizing the cycle-averaged risk gives $\omega^* = (4\nu^2 \Sigma / c')^{1/3}$, $c' = \sigma^2 d_{\mathrm{eff}}(\rho)$, and the plug-in strength $\rho^* = \sigma^2 / (n\delta^2)$. A random-matrix deterministic equivalent extends both laws to finite dimension, renormalizing the anchor to $\rho_{\mathrm{eff}} = \rho (e^{\zeta q} - 1) / (\zeta q)$; it matches simulation within 5% at fixed operating points and within 13% at the method's own, and rank-deficient populations reduce exactly to their active subspace. The resulting method, SPAR, calibrates window and strength online from residuals. On a 27-configuration grid the calibrated window opens on drift without divergence, and the grid defaults transfer to an hourly electricity stream and to BCI IV 2b. The core algebra, refresh chain, and regret bounds are formalized in Lean 4.

title: CAFIN: CUDA-accelerated Adaptive Fisher Information Matrix Network Optimization via GPU-Native Kernel Fusion
authors: Maryam Arshad, Muhammad Khuram Shahzad
abstract: Second-order optimizers improve deep neural network training using curvature information, but their practical efficiency is limited by GPU execution overhead. AdaFisher reduces Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) approximation costs through diagonal Kronecker structures and exponential moving averages, yet its PyTorch implementation requires sequential CUDA kernel launches, intermediate tensor allocations, and repeated memory accesses. We introduce CAFIN, a GPU-native CUDA kernel fusion framework that improves AdaFisher execution efficiency without changing its optimization formulation. The proposed approach progressively integrates FIM preconditioner construction, exponential moving average updates, gradient preconditioning, momentum accumulation, weight decay, and parameter updates into fused CUDA kernels. Shared-memory reuse, register-resident computation, and in-place operations further reduce memory traffic and intermediate allocations. Experiments using ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet across NVIDIA GTX 1660 Ti and RTX 3060 Laptop GPUs demonstrate up to 78.4% lower isolated FIM construction latency and 2.1-26.9% lower optimizer-step latency. The implementation also eliminates approximately 18.91 MB of intermediate GPU memory allocations per optimizer step. Numerical validation confirms consistency within the predefined FP32 tolerance, while convergence accuracy remains comparable across evaluated datasets and random seeds. These findings demonstrate that CUDA kernel fusion can substantially accelerate second-order optimization while preserving AdaFisher's underlying mathematical formulation and learning behavior.

title: An Asynchronous Federated Learning Platform for Lung Adenocarcinoma Grading via Foundation Models and Structural Pruning
authors: Moon-Il Joo, Md Ariful Islam Mozumder, Hee-Cheol Kim
abstract: Classification of lung adenocarcinoma into poorly differentiated (PD) and well-to-moderately differentiated (WMD) subtypes plays an important role in patient survival; however, consistent classification is difficult due to inter-observer variability among pathologists. Collecting data from multiple hospitals is also challenging due to patient privacy concerns. This study proposes a web-based federated learning system that shares only locally trained model weights without sharing patient data between institutions. The UNI2 foundation model and CLAM-SB were used to classify pathological whole slide images. A four-client federated learning system was constructed, and the NLST cohort was reserved exclusively for external validation. In centralized evaluation, joint training with CPTAC and TCGA outperformed single-institution training on external validation, confirming the necessity of multi-institutional data integration. FedAvg, FedProx, FedBN, and FedNova were compared as federated learning algorithms under identical experimental conditions. Test AUC ranked as FedBN, FedProx, FedNova, and FedAvg. FedNova showed the most balanced classification performance between PD and WMD. L1-norm structural pruning at 20%, 30%, and 40% sparsity was applied to reduce model transmission size. FedAvg, FedProx, and FedBN showed a tendency of decreasing Test AUC under pruning, while FedNova achieved improved Test AUC across all sparsity levels. A web-based application was developed supporting slide upload, local training, AI classification, and attention heatmap-based visualization. The combination of FedNova and 40% pruning was confirmed as a practical approach that improves communication efficiency and classification performance while protecting patient privacy.

title: Multi-Step Underwater Acoustic Channel Prediction via Dual-Domain Structure Preservation and Pretrained Transformer
authors: Mingjie Cao, Gewei Zhang, Deqing Wang, Lizhao You, Fei-Yun Wu, Liqun Fu
abstract: Accurate future channel state information (CSI) is essential for underwater acoustic (UWA) communication because delays associated with signal propagation, feedback, scheduling, and transceiver reconfiguration can render currently available CSI outdated. However, most existing predictors estimate only the next channel state and obtain multi-step forecasts through recursive rollout, which causes prediction errors to accumulate as the multipath structure evolves. The scarcity of sea-trial measurements further limits reliable model training. To address these challenges, we propose LLM4UACP, a dual-domain, structure-preserving framework that adapts a pretrained Transformer for few-shot multi-step UWA channel prediction. LLM4UACP extracts complementary features from the channel impulse response (CIR) and channel frequency response (CFR), aligns them through Fourier-consistent fusion, and encodes the fused representation as delay-time tokens. A pretrained Transformer with a frozen backbone is adapted through Butterfly Orthogonal Fine-tuning to jointly predict multiple future CIRs in a single forward pass, thereby avoiding the error accumulation associated with recursive prediction. Experiments on the measured SO-06 and SO-07 channels show that LLM4UACP achieves normalized mean squared error (NMSE) values of 0.0411 and 0.0399, corresponding to reductions of 88.53% and 85.15%, respectively, relative to the most recent baseline. With only 0.11M trainable parameters, LLM4UACP maintains robust performance across varying prediction horizons and observation-window lengths, limited-data settings, and cross-dataset transfer scenarios.

title: Adversarial Risk in the Generative AI Era Necessitates Dropping the Small Epsilon Ball
authors: Andrew C. Cullen, Neil G. Marchant, Paul Montague, Jiani Xie, Benjamin I. P. Rubinstein
abstract: Adversarial Machine Learning research is currently centered on the search for the epsilon-ball: minimal perturbations designed to fool models while remaining imperceptible to humans. We argue that this fixation on $\ell_p$ norms is a metrological trap that communicates a distorted perception of risk to defenders, one that is unaligned with real-world system vulnerabilities. This paradigm misleads defenders into optimizing for narrow, mathematical robustness at the expense of systemic security, while simultaneously incentivizing attackers to exploit non-overlapping alternative adversarial pathways. Ultimately, we argue that the dominance of the $\ell_p$ ball does not just fail to reduce harm---it may actively facilitate it by communicating a false sense of security against the wrong threats.

title: StructRL: Model-Free Reinforcement Learning with Replay Graphs
authors: Ivo Nowak
abstract: StructRL turns the experience collected during reinforcement learning into an explicit replay graph. Once the graph contains a path to the task goal, dynamic programming selects actions on the observed part of the state space; these actions form a graph policy that is defined only where the required transitions have been observed. StructRL transfers these actions to model-free learners: as action preferences for a DQN Q-model and as target directions along shortest observed paths for a SAC actor. For DQN on three sparse-reward MiniGrid tasks, final success rises from 0.10 to 0.90 (DoorKey), 0.10 to 0.80 (KeyCorridor) and 0 to 0.50 (ObstructedMaze); plain DQN does not catch up with three times the budget. For SAC on continuous PointMaze, graph-derived direction labels raise final success from 0.17 to 1.0 on seven matched runs that reached the goal. Distilling the graph policy into a fresh Q-model gives a DoorKey 6x6 controller that reaches the goal from 91% of reachable states, against 38% for plain DQN. Scaling experiments identify three bottlenecks: incomplete graph support, structural aliasing, and loss of graph information in high-dimensional inputs.

title: An Eyring-Kramers Formula for Singular Wells
authors: Yingli Wang, Lingjiong Zhu
abstract: Understanding the persistence of learned behaviors in AI safety motivates an investigation of the dynamical counterpart to the equilibrium geometry studied in singular learning theory. We analyze this persistence through transitions between singular wells. We establish an Eyring-Kramers formula for a low temperature Langevin diffusion between two compact connected zero components of a real-analytic potential. The wells may be singular and nonisolated, and the unique minimizing gate is a nondegenerate index-one saddle, with gates understood as inclusion-minimal sets meeting every minimizing path. A boundary-gate construction shows that uniqueness of this inclusion-minimal gate is equivalent to every minimizing path passing through the saddle and one such path meeting the communication level only there. Compact semianalytic topology provides a separating function away from a fixed saddle neighborhood; analytic Morse coordinates give matching capacity bounds by first sending the temperature to zero and then shrinking that neighborhood. An anchored energy estimate and a small-ball potential-theoretic identity give uniformity for deterministic starting points. The leading constant is expressed in terms of the sublevel-volume coefficient, a Gamma factor, and the saddle Hessian.

title: KernelMosaic: An Open Dataset and Agentic Framework for CUDA Kernel Generation
authors: Ningyuan Xi, Yuhang Lai, Ning Miao
abstract: Training large language models to generate efficient CUDA kernels requires supervision spanning diverse computational requirements and iterative code optimization. Constructing this supervision is challenging because of heterogeneous specifications, and useful implementations emerge through iterative complicated testing and refinement. We introduce KernelMosaic, an open dataset pairing diverse CUDA tasks with verified solutions and trajectories. Human-guided review and diversity-aware selection curate tasks expressed as natural-language descriptions, reference programs, mathematical specifications, and their intersections. To build the solutions and trajectories, our agentic framework guides a strong LLM through implementation, correctness repair, and performance optimization with reusable CUDA guidance and execution feedback. Supervised fine-tuning of a small open-source model on KernelMosaic raises correctness from 4%, 0%, and 0% to 88%, 82%, and 16% on KernelBench L1, L2, and L3, respectively, while increasing the fraction of tasks with kernels faster than PyTorch eager at every level. Further training experiments show that supervision from the curated trajectories substantially outperforms direct responses and promotes sustained testing and revision. These results demonstrate that KernelMosaic enables a general-purpose model to achieve substantial gains in CUDA kernel generation.

title: Evaluating AI Musical Creativity: Towards a Quantitative Multi-Dimensional Framework Based on Value, Novelty, and Surprise
authors: Hindy Rossignol, Giorgio Franceschelli, Mirco Musolesi
abstract: Despite the increasing sophistication of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI), research on the evaluation of AI-generated musical creativity remains limited. To address this gap, this paper proposes a quantitative framework for the formalization and evaluation of AI musical creativity. Building on Margaret Boden's theory, which conceptualizes creativity in terms of value, novelty, and surprise, the framework adapts and operationalizes these three dimensions for the musical domain. On the hypothesis that certain aspects of musical creativity can be assessed with a degree of objectivity, a domain-specific set of quantitative metrics for evaluating the creativity of AI-generated music is introduced. Rather than reducing musical creativity to a single unifying measure, this article proposes an ensemble of complementary metrics that capture its different dimensions, recognizing the complexity of musical artifacts and the difficulty of defining meaningful multi-objective compositional criteria. The framework has two implications. First, it gives researchers and developers a principled methodology and quantitative tools for empirically evaluating creative outputs, enabling more informed model development and reducing unnecessary computational costs. Second, it lays the groundwork for future generative models to optimize directly for creativity by adopting these metrics as learning objectives.

title: Evaluating the Performance of LLMs in Drafting NIH Data Management Plans
authors: Nahid Zeinali, James ONeil, Xuebin Dong, Rebecca Hofstein Grady, Maria Praetzellis, Brian Riley, John Chodacki, Bhavesh Patel
abstract: Sharing research data is essential to promote transparency, enable reproducibility, and fuel scientific discoveries. To ensure consistent sharing, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and other funding agencies require applicants to submit data management plans (DMPs) with their proposals. They aim to encourage researchers to consider their data management and sharing strategies early on. However, researchers often face challenges when developing DMPs due to a lack of knowledge about data-sharing practices. Here, we evaluated the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) in drafting DMPs compliant with the 2023 NIH guidelines. The goal was to investigate whether LLM-supported DMP creation could reduce the burden on researchers and librarians. We compared Llama and GPT performance against NIH-provided DMP samples. We also asked domain experts to evaluate LLM-generated DMPs. Overall, we found that LLMs can accelerate the creation of initial drafts but still require expert review before submission to ensure clarity and completeness. Moreover, open-source LLMs may not be as ready off-the-shelf as commercial ones for drafting funder-compliant DMPs.

title: Multiple-Choice Secretary Problem with Predictions
authors: Jing Yuan, Qi Cai, Xin Gao, Shaojie Tang
abstract: We study the multiple-choice secretary problem, in which candidates arrive in uniformly random order and the goal is to select at most $k$ candidates to maximize their total value. We consider a setting where predictions of individual candidate values are available before any candidate arrives. Fujii and Yoshida's Learned Kleinberg algorithm achieves competitive loss $O(\min\{\log k/\sqrt{k},\eps\})$, where $k$ is the selection capacity and $\eps$ is the maximum multiplicative prediction error. We remove the logarithmic factor through a sharper analysis of the same switching algorithm with a retuned threshold. The resulting competitive ratio is at least $\max\{0,1-\min\{32/\sqrt{k},4\eps\}\}$. In particular, exact predictions ($\eps=0$) achieve the offline optimum on every arrival order.

title: Cleaning an Agent's History Hurts When the World Still Holds the Error
authors: Egor Pakhomov, Anurag Koul, Hongjun Liu, Bo Pang, Shafiq Joty, Erik Nijkamp
abstract: Tool-using language-model agents accumulate histories of their own mistakes, and a system that compacts, repairs or hands off such a history decides what it says about those mistakes while their effects stay in the world. Prior work cleans the history at a fixed world, where showing a corrected step and saying it is done move together. We ask whether the same correct content helps or hurts depending on how the history states it and what the world holds. We freeze an agent mid-task with its exact world state, edit the history or the world, and let a receiver model continue. On AgentCE-Bench, after the agent commits a wrong value, we hold the world fixed and add the correct value by two natural edits: a truthful note beside the preserved error or the agent's own completed action. The note raises recovery, the share of remaining targets the receiver gets right, from 51% under a matched neutral note to 66%. The completed action lowers it below the unedited history, from 50% to 44%, so the value's presence alone does not predict the effect. On AppWorld, after a database write, we vary whether its receipt reports success or failure and whether its effect is present. A success receipt lowers whole-task success from 45% to 28% while the effect is absent and raises it from 38% to 49% once present. The two effects differ by 27 points pooled over two receivers, a difference positive in six of eight receivers at 97.5% and seven at 95%. A history edit's effect thus depends on the world it describes, and a history made to look clean while the world still holds the error can leave an agent worse off than no edit at all.

title: Thompson Sampling using Prior-fitted Diffusion Transformers
authors: Sihwa Park, Jingsen Zhu, Vinamr Jain, Sheng-Yen Chou, Alexander Terenin
abstract: Thompson sampling is natural randomized strategy for optimizing unknown functions in a black-box manner. In continuous global optimization, Thompson sampling has largely been restricted to Gaussian process priors, as these are essentially the only class for which computing the posterior distribution has been tractable in practice. In this work, we introduce \emph{prior-fitted diffusion transformers}, which are diffusion models that perform Thompson sampling in-context at inference time, after being pre-trained using the prior-fitted network paradigm. To apply these models, we develop a set of practical non-Gaussian priors for general black-box functions---including those that have characteristics that cannot be achieved under Gaussianity, such as priors over unimodal functions. We also quantify the tradeoff between model size and the number of pre-training iterations, and show that these models follow scaling laws akin to those observed in transformers defined over other modalities. Across a set of global optimization benchmarks, we show that prior-fitted diffusion transformers with non-Gaussian priors can achieve improved performance compared to traditional pipelines built on Gaussian processes.

title: Closing the Loop: Co-Evolving EM for Irregular Time Series Generation in Lifted Representations
authors: Idan Arbiv, Gal Fadlon, Omri Azencot
abstract: Regular time-series generation from irregular time series is typically reduced to one-shot imputation: complete each partial sequence once, freeze the completions, and train a generator on the resulting surrogate dataset. We show that this open-loop strategy is structurally flawed. Point imputers collapse ambiguous missing regions to conditional averages, while stochastic imputers become stale as the generator evolves; the binding constraint is therefore iteration, not imputer design. We introduce a co-evolving Monte Carlo EM framework that closes the imputer-generator loop. Each E-step samples missing values from the posterior of the current generator, and each M-step retrains the generator on these completions, preserving unconditional generator training. Since our diffusion prior operates in a lifted 2D representation while observations live in time-series space, we further introduce Posterior Sampling for Lifted Representations (PSLR), which enforces operator-consistent conditioning, uncertainty preservation, and manifold consistency during the E-step. Across ten datasets and four corruption regimes, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving over the strongest baselines by 59% in discriminative score, 15% in predictive score, 73% in Context-FID, and 71% in feature-correlation error. Ablations show that our approach reduces average discriminative score by 73% over single-step baselines, closing most of the remaining gap to the clean-data oracle. Code is available at https://github.com/azencot-group/PSLR.

title: Abstention Is Not Threshold Compliance: Stated Scoring Rules in Open Language Models
authors: Dongsun Moon
abstract: Kalai et al. propose stating the scoring rule in the prompt with an explicit threshold t, so that a model should answer only when its probability of being correct exceeds t.
